rules.name: Dropping payload via certutil
rules.description:
BazaCall is a campaign that manipulate users into calling a customer support center, where they are instructed to download an Excel file to unsubscribe from a phony service. When the user opens the Excel file, they are prompted to enable a malicious macro that infects their device with BazaLoader.
This query hunts for an attacker-created copy of certutil.exe, a legitimate process, which the macro uses to download BazaLoader.
rules.oci_query: 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' and ('Parent Process Name' != 'certutil.exe') and ('Parent Process Name' != 'cmd.exe') and (('Command Line' like '*-urlcache*' and 'Command Line' like '*split*' and 'Command Line' like '*http*'))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Dropping Payload via certutil
rules.description: BazaCall campaign tricks users into calling a fake customer support center, and download a malicious Excel file which contains a macro to infect users' device with BazaLoader. This query searches for a copy of certutil.exe used by the macro.
rules.oci_query: 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' and ('Parent Process Name' != 'certutil.exe') and ('Parent Process Name' != 'cmd.exe') and (('Command Line' like '*-urlcache*' and 'Command Line' like '*split*' and 'Command Line' like '*http*'))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Electron-CVE-2018-1000006
rules.description:
The query checks process command lines arguments and parent/child combinations to find machines where there have been.
Attempts to exploit the Protocol Handler Vulnerability of Electron framework CVE-2018-1000006.
Electron is a common framework used by many popular applications (e.g. Skype, Teams, Slack, VSCode) which expose protocol handlers.
Which can trigger a remote code execution vulnerability via a browser vector (e.g. Chrome, Internet Explorer, Edge).
CVE: CVE-2018-1000006.
Read more here:.
Https://electronjs.org/blog/protocol-handler-fix.
Https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2018-1000006.
Https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/43899.
Https://hackernoon.com/exploiting-electron-rce-in-exodus-wallet-d9e6db13c374.
Tags: #exploit #CVE-2018-1000006 #Electron.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ('Process Name' in ('code.exe', 'skype.exe', 'slack.exe', 'teams.exe')) and ('Parent Process Name' in ('iexplore.exe', 'runtimebroker.exe', 'chrome.exe')) and ('Command Line' like '*--gpu-launcher*') | stats min(Time) as FirstEvent, max(Time) as LastEvent by 'Host Name (Server)', 'Command Line', 'Process Name', 'Parent Process Name'
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: exchange-powershell-snapin-loaded
rules.description:
This query was originally published in the threat analytics report, "Exchange Server zero-days exploited in the wild".
In early March 2021, Microsoft released patches for four different zero-day vulnerabilities affecting Microsoft Exchange Server. The vulnerabilities were being used in a coordinated attack. For more information on the vulnerabilities, visit the following links:
1. CVE-2021-26855
2. CVE-2021-26857
3. CVE-2021-26858
4. CVE-2021-27065
The following query finds evidence of an Exchange PowerShell snap-in being loaded. This can indicate an attempt to exfiltrate data.
More queries related to this threat can be found under the See also section of this page.
Reference - https://msrc-blog.microsoft.com/2021/03/02/multiple-security-updates-released-for-exchange-server/
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and (('Process Name' like '*cmd.exe*' or 'Process Name' like '*powershell.exe*' or 'Process Name' like '*PowerShell_ISE.exe*')) and ('Command Line' like '*Add-PSSnapin Microsoft.Exchange.Powershell.Snapin*')
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Exchange IIS Worker Dropping Webshells
rules.description: This query checks for the IIS worker process dropping files that resemble web shells and other artifacts seen in known attacks. Reference: https://msrc-blog.microsoft.com/2021/03/02/multiple-security-updates-released-for-exchange-server
rules.oci_query: 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' and ('Parent Process Name' = 'w3wp.exe') and ('Command Line' like '*MSExchange*') and (('Target Filename' like '*\\\\\\\\wwwroot\\\\\\\\*' or 'Target Filename' like '*HttpProxy\\\\\\\\owa\\\\\\\\*' or 'Target Filename' like '*\\\\\\\\Temporary ASP.NET Files\\\\\\\\*')) and (not(('Target Filename' like '*\\\\\\\\tmp\\\\\\\\*' or 'Target Filename' like '*\\\\\\\\dl3\\\\\\\\*'))) and (not ('Target Filename' like '*.log')) and (not ('Target Filename' like '*.json')) and (not ('Target Filename' like '*.ini')) and (not ('Target Filename' like '*.vb')) and (not ('Target Filename' like '*.tmp')) and (not ('Target Filename' like '*.xml')) and (not ('Target Filename' like '*.js'))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: ExecuteBase64DecodedPayload
rules.description:
Process executed from binary hidden in Base64 encoded file.  Encoding malicious software is a.
Technique to obfuscate files from detection.
The first and second ProcessCommandLine component is looking for Python decoding base64.
The third ProcesssCommandLine component is looking for the Bash/sh commandline base64 decoding tool.
The fourth one is looking for Ruby decoding base64.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ('Command Line' like '*.decode(\'base64\')*' or 'Command Line' like '*.b64decode(*' or 'Command Line' like '*base64 --decode*' or 'Command Line' like '*.decode64(*') | fields Time, 'Host Name (Server)', 'Process Name', 'Target Filename', 'Command Line', 'Command Line' | sort -Time | head 100
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: ExploitGuardBlockOfficeChildProcess
rules.description:
These queries check telemetry from the Exploit Guard rule: Rule: Block Office applications from creating child processes.
(Rule ID d4f940ab-401b-4efc-aadc-ad5f3c50688a).
Read more about it here: https://docs.microsoft.com/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-exploit-guard/attack-surface-reduction-exploit-guard.
Oftentimes organizations enable this rule in audit mode and check the results before setting block mode.
You can use query #2 to measure the rule impact on your network in audit mode before turning it to block mode.
Query #1 is used after setting it to block mode - to analyze the block stats.
Tags: #ASR.
Query #1: block stats.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and (Action = 'AsrOfficeChildProcessBlocked') | eval BlockedProcess = 'Process Name' | eval ParentProcess = 'Parent Process Name' | fields BlockedProcess, ParentProcess, 'Host Name (Server)' | stats distinctcount('Host Name (Server)') as MachineCount, count as RuleHits by BlockedProcess, ParentProcess | sort -MachineCount
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: hiding-java-class-file
rules.description:
This query was originally published in the threat analytics report, Adwind utilizes Java for cross-platform impact.
Adwind is a remote access tool (RAT) that takes advantage of the cross-platform capabilities of the Java framework. It can check which operating system a target is running and adapt accordingly, allowing it to successfully compromise both Windows and macOS devices.
The query below checks for attempts to disguise Java class files (i.e., complied code with a .class extension). Although the behavior detected by this query is typical of attacks that use Adwind malware, unrelated attacks may use the same or similar defense evasion techniques.
See Detecting a JAR attachment for an additional query that detects behavior associated with Adwind attacks.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs') and ('Command Line' like '*attrib +h +s +r *' and 'Command Line' like '*.class*')
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: insider-threat-detection-queries (12)
rules.description:
Intent:
- Use MTP capability to look for insider threat potential risk indicators
- Indicators would then serve as the building block for insider threat risk modeling in subsequent tools
Definition of Insider Threat:
"The potential for an individual who has or had authorized access to an organization's assets to use their access, either maliciously or unintentionally, to act in a way that could negatively affect the organization."
This collection of queries describes the different indicators that could be used to model and look for patterns suggesting an increased risk of an individual becoming a potential insider threat.
Note: no single indicator should be used as a lone determinant of insider threat activity, but should be part of an overall program to understand the increased risk to your organization's critical assets. This in turn is used to feed an investigation by a formal insider threat program to look at the context associated with the whole person to understand the implication of a set of indicators.
rules.oci_query: 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' and (Action = 'UserAccountCreated')
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: java-executing-cmd-to-run-powershell
rules.description:
This query was originally published in the threat analytics report, Sysrv botnet evolution.
Sysrv is a Go-based botnet that targets both Windows and Linux servers, and steals resources to mine cryptocurrency.
The following query finds instances of the Java process being used to execute cmd.exe, and download and execute a PowerShell script.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ('Parent Process Name' = 'java.exe' and 'Process Name' = 'cmd.exe' and ('Command Line' like '*powershell iex*' and 'Command Line' like '*DownloadString*'))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: jse-launched-by-word
rules.description:
This query was originally published in the threat analytics report, Emulation-evading JavaScripts.
Attackers in several ransomware campaigns have employed heavily obfuscated JavaScript code, in order to implant malware or execute malicious commands. The obfuscation is intended to help the code evade security systems and potentially escape sandbox environments.
The following query detects when Word or File Explorer have launched files with a .jse extension. Attackers involved in various human-operated campaigns have been known to embed a heavily obfuscated JavaScript file in malicious Word docs. The loader is used to download and install the banking trojan, Trickbot.
See Detect .jse file creation events for a similar technique.
Reference - https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/03/05/human-operated-ransomware-attacks-a-preventable-disaster/

rules.name: launching-cmd-echo[Nobelium]
rules.description:
This query was originally published in the threat analytics report, Solorigate supply chain attack. Please note that these attacks are currently known as the Nobelium campaign.
Microsoft detects the 2020 SolarWinds supply chain attack implant and its other components as part of a campaign by the Nobelium activity group. Nobelium is the threat actor behind the attack against SolarWinds, which was previously referred to as Solorigate.
Nobelium silently added malicious code to legitimate software updates for Orion, which is IT monitoring software provided by SolarWinds. In this way, malicious dynamic link libraries (DLLs) were distributed to SolarWinds customers.
The following query detects events when SolarWinds processes attempted to launch the cmd.exe command prompt using the 'echo' command. Using 'echo' in this way is suspicious, as it is an indirect way of issuing commands, and may not be readily detected by certain kinds of security solutions.

https://docs.microsoft.com/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/cmd
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ('Parent Process Name' = 'SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe') and ('Process Name' = 'cmd.exe' and 'Command Line' like '*echo*')

rules.name: lazagne
rules.description:
This query was originally published in the threat analytics report, Ryuk ransomware. There is also a related blog.
Ryuk is human-operated ransomware. Much like DoppelPaymer ransomware, Ryuk is spread manually, often on networks that are already infected with Trickbot.
During a typical Ryuk campaign, an operator will use LaZagne, a credential theft tool, to access stored passwords for service accounts. The accounts are then used to jump from desktop clients to servers or domain controllers, allowing for better reconnaissance, faster movement, and a more severe impact on the target.
The following query detects credential theft by LaZagne.
The See also section below lists links to other queries associated with Ryuk ransomware.
References:
https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/03/05/human-operated-ransomware-attacks-a-preventable-disaster/
https://www.microsoft.com/wdsi/threats/malware-encyclopedia-description?Name=Ransom:Win32/Ryuk&threatId=-2147232689
https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/03/05/human-operated-ransomware-attacks-a-preventable-disaster/
https://github.com/AlessandroZ/LaZagne
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ('Process Name' = 'reg.exe' and 'Command Line' like '*save*' and 'Command Line' like '*hklm*' and 'Command Line' like '*sam*') | fields Entity, Time, 'Process ID', 'Parent Process Name', 'Process ID', 'Process Name', 'Command Line'
rules.author: Upstream contributors

Using it, a malicious attacker could use this flaw to execute arbitrary commands with root privileges.
CVE: CVE-2018-1111.
Read more here:.
Https://access.redhat.com/security/cve/cve-2018-1111.
Https://www.cvedetails.com/cve/CVE-2018-1111.

rules.name: Microsoft Entra ID Local Device Join Information and Transport Key Registry Keys Access
rules.description:
'This detection uses Windows security events to detect suspicious access attempts by the same process to registry keys that provide information about an Microsoft Entra ID joined or registered devices and Transport keys (tkpub / tkpriv).
 This information can be used to export the Device Certificate (dkpub / dkpriv) and Transport key (tkpub/tkpriv).
 These set of keys can be used to impersonate existing Microsoft Entra ID joined devices.
 This detection requires an access control entry (ACE) on the system access control list (SACL) of the following securable objects:
 HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\CloudDomainJoin (Microsoft Entra ID joined devices)
 HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\WorkplaceJoin (Microsoft Entra ID registered devices)
 HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Cryptography\Ngc\KeyTransportKey (Transport Key)
 Make sure you set the SACL to propagate to its sub-keys. You can find more information in here https://github.com/OTRF/Set-AuditRule/blob/master/rules/registry/aad_connect_health_service_agent.yml
 Reference: https://aadinternals.com/post/deviceidentity/'
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Security Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Event Security Logs')
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Security Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Event Security Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Event System Logs')

rules.name: office-apps-launching-wscipt
rules.description:
This query was originally published in the threat analytics report, Trickbot: Pervasive & underestimated.
Trickbot is a very prevalent piece of malware with an array of malicious capabilities. Originally designed to steal banking credentials, it has since evolved into a modular trojan that can deploy other malware, disable security software, and perform command-and-control (C2) operations.
Trickbot is frequently spread through email. An attacker will send a target a message with an attachment containing a malicious macro. If the target enables the macro, it will write a JScript Encoded (JSE) file to disk (JScript is a Microsoft dialect of ECMAScript). The JSE file will then be launched using wscript.exe to perform a variety of malicious tasks, particularly reconnaissance.
The following query detects when Office applications have launched wscript.exe to run a JSE file.
See Detect rundll.exe being used for reconnaissance and command-and-control for another query related to Trickbot activity.
Reference - https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0266/
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Security Events') and ('Parent Process Name' in ('winword.exe', 'excel.exe', 'outlook.exe')) and ('Process Name' = 'wscript.exe' and 'Command Line' like '*.jse*')
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.description:

Trickbot is a very prevalent piece of malware with an array of malicious capabilities. Originally designed to steal banking credentials, it has since evolved into a modular trojan that can deploy other malware, disable security software, and perform command-and-control (C2) operations.
Trickbot is frequently spread through email. An attacker will send a target a message with an attachment containing a malicious macro. If the target enables the macro, it will write a JScript Encoded (JSE) file to disk (JScript is a Microsoft dialect of ECMAScript). The JSE file will then be launched using wscript.exe to perform a variety of malicious tasks, particularly reconnaissance.

rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Office ASR rule triggered from browser spawned office process.
rules.description:
The attacker sends a spearphishing email to a user. The email contains a link which points to a website that eventually presents the user a download of an MS Office document. This document contains a malicious macro. The macro triggers one of the ASR rules. 
This detection looks for Office ASR violations triggered by an Office document opened from a browser.
Note: be aware that you need to have the proper ASR rules enabled for this detection to work.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and (Action like '*Office*') and ('Parent Process Name' in ('iexplore.exe', 'chrome.exe', 'firefox.exe', 'msedge.exe') or 'Parent Process Name' in ('iexplore.exe', 'chrome.exe', 'firefox.exe', 'msedge.exe')) and (not('Process Name' like '*.docx' or 'Process Name' like '*.xlsx' or 'Process Name' like '*.pptx'))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: powercat-download

4. CVE-2021-27065

MANY OF THE FILES THAT SHOULD COME UP HERE MAY BE LEGIT. Unsigned files
or ones that don't have any relations to printers that you are using are
suspicious.
Second query that can be used for finding client machines that
could be operating print servers or file servers is also included here.

incoming traffic to the SMB or EPMAP Ports (445) if you need to keep the
spooler service running to print from clients.

rules.description:
Private Key Files.
This query identifies file operation with files having.
One of the extensions commonly used to save a private.
Key.  The risk is that if an attacker were to obtain.
The file, they could brute force any password on it.
And potentially obtain a powerful certificate.  To do.
This, they would only need to obtain read access to.
The file.
The risk associated with these files is heavily.
Determined by the value of the certificate.  For example,.
Loss of a self-signed certificate created by Adobe Acrobat.
Is significantly less impactful than loss of a website.
SSL certificate.
Recommendation: Know where these files are, and if possible.
Back them up and remove them.  You might also consider.
Creating an informational alert.

rules.name: recon-with-rundll
rules.description:
This query was originally published in the threat analytics report, Trickbot: Pervasive & underestimated.
Trickbot is a very prevalent piece of malware with an array of malicious capabilities. Originally designed to steal banking credentials, it has since evolved into a modular trojan that can deploy other malware, disable security software, and perform command and control (C2) operations.
Trickbot operators are known to use the legitimate Windows process rundll.exe to perform malicious activities, such as reconnaissance. Once a target is infected, the operator will drop a batch file that runs several commands and connects to a C2 server for further action.
The following query detects suspicious rundll.exe activity associated with Trickbot campaigns.
See Office applications launching wscript.exe to run JScript for another query related to Trickbot activity.
Reference - https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0266/
rules.oci_query: 'Log Source' = 'SOC Sysmon Network Logs' and ('Parent Process Name' = 'rundll32.exe') and ('Command Line' like '*rundll32.exe*' and not ('Command Line' like '* *') and 'Command Line' != '') | timestats span = 5minute distinctcount('Destination IP') as DestinationIPCount, unique('Destination IP') as set_RemoteIP, unique('Request URL') as set_RemoteUrl, unique('Destination Port') as set_RemotePort by 'Command Line', Entity
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Recon with Rundll
rules.description: This query detects suspicious rundll.exe activity associated with Trickbot campaigns.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Network Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Sysmon Network Logs') and ('Parent Process Name' = 'rundll32.exe') and ('Command Line' like '*rundll32.exe*' and not ('Command Line' like '* *') and 'Command Line' != '') | timestats span = 5minute distinctcount('Destination IP') as DestinationIPCount, unique('Destination IP') as set_RemoteIP, unique('Request URL') as set_RemoteUrl, unique('Destination Port') as set_RemotePort by 'Command Line', Entity
rules.author: Upstream contributors

The query below can help locate a reverse shell established by an attacker. The command the query searches for is associated with, but not definitely indicative of, EvilQuest infections.
Other queries related to EvilQuest ransomware can be found under the See also section below.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs') and ('Command Line' like '*bash -i >& /dev/tcp/*')

Robbinhood is ransomware that has been involved in several high-profile incidents, including a 2019 attack on the city of Baltimore, Maryland. Robbinhood operators often employ a distinctive defense evasion technique, where they load a vulnerable driver on to a target and exploit it, in order to turn off security software -- essentially using the driver as malware.
The following query detects if a device contains the vulnerable drivers. These are often, but not always, implanted on the target by operators seeking to use this technique to turn off security software.
For a query that detects a later stage of this technique, see Detect security evasion related to the Robbinhood ransomware campaign.

https://www.nytimes.com/2019/05/22/us/baltimore-ransomware.html

rules.name: snip3-encoded-powershell-structure
rules.description:
Snip3 is a family of related remote access trojans. Although the malware in this family contain numerous small variations, they all exhibit similar behaviors and techniques.
The following query looks for the method that Snip3 malware use to obfuscate PowerShell commands with UTF8 encoding. This technique is intended to evade detection from security products, and avoids the more standard switches used for encoding in malware such as Emotet.
At present, this method of encoding is much more rare, being seen largely with loader installation of RevengeRAT, AsyncRAT and other RATs used in campaigns targeting the aviation industry.
rules.oci_query: 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' and ('Parent Process Name' = 'powershell.exe') and (('Command Line' like '*IEX*' and 'Command Line' like '*Text.Encoding*' and 'Command Line' like '*UTF8.GetString(@*')) and (('Command Line' like '*Unrestricted*' or 'Command Line' like '*Hidden*'))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: snip3-malicious-network-connectivity
rules.description:
Snip3 is a family of related remote access trojans. Although the malware in this family contain numerous small variations, they all exhibit similar behaviors and techniques.
The following query looks for potentially hollowed processes that may be used to facilitate command-and-control or exfiltration by Snip3 malware. This technique has been used in recent cases to exfiltrate data, including credentials.
The query may return additional malware or campaigns not necessarily associated with Snip3. However, Microsoft recommends triaging all non-benign results as potential malware.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Network Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Sysmon Network Logs') and ('Parent Process Name' in ('RegSvcs.exe', 'RegAsm.exe', 'InstallUtil.exe')) and ('Command Line' in ('\\"RegAsm.exe\\"', '\\"RegSvcs.exe\\"', '\\"InstallUtil.exe\\"')) and ('Parent Process Name' like '*Powershell.exe')
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: snip3-revengerat-c2-exfiltration

The following query looks for network connections using any protocols associated with recent RevengeRAT, AsyncRAT, and other malware campaigns targeting the aviation industry.
This activity is often followed by connections to copy-and-paste sites such as pastebin.com, stikked.ch, academia.edu, and archive.org. Many of these connections will occur on non-standard ports.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Network Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Sysmon Network Logs') and ('Request URL' in ('mail.alamdarhardware.com', 'kexa600200.ddns.net', 'h0pe1759.ddns.net', 'n0ahark2021.ddns.net', ' kimjoy007.dyndns.org', ' kimjoy.ddns.net', ' asin8988.ddns.net', ' asin8989.ddns.net', 'asin8990.ddns.net'))

rules.name: tomcat-8-executing-powershell
rules.description:

Sysrv is a Go-based botnet that targets both Windows and Linux servers, and steals resources to mine cryptocurrency.
The following query finds instances of Apache Tomcat 8 being exploited to execute encoded PowerShell commands.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ('Parent Process Name' like 'tomcat*') and ('Parent Process Name' in ('cmd.exe', 'powershell.exe') and 'Command Line' like '-enc *' and ('Command Line' like '*cmd.exe*' or 'Command Line' like '*powershell.exe*' or 'Command Line' like '*sc.exe*' or 'Command Line' like '*schtasks.exe*' or 'Command Line' like '*WMIC.exe*'))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Top 10 External Senders (Malware)
rules.description:
Identifies the top 10 external sender addresses delivering inbound emails classified as malware.
If you want to exclude your own organization's domains (including subdomains), add a filter after the malware filter, e.g.:
  | where SenderFromAddress !contains ".yourdomain.com"
(Replace "yourdomain.com" with your actual domain.)
Based on Defender for Office 365 workbook: https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/blog/microsoftdefenderforoffice365blog/part-2-build-custom-email-security-reports-and-dashboards-with-workbooks-in-micr/4411303

rules.name: turn-off-system-restore
rules.description:
This query was originally published in the threat analytics report, Ransomware continues to hit healthcare, critical services. There is also a related blog.
In April of 2020, security researchers observed multiple ransomware campaigns using the same set of techniques.
The following query detects attempts to stop System Restore, which would prevent the user from recovering data by going back to a restore point.
The See also section below lists more queries related to techniques shared by these campaigns.
Reference - https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/2020/04/28/ransomware-groups-continue-to-target-healthcare-critical-services-heres-how-to-reduce-risk/
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ('Parent Process Name' = 'rundll32.exe' and not ('Command Line' like '* *') and 'Command Line' != '' and 'Process Name' in ('schtasks.exe') and 'Command Line' like '*Change*' and 'Command Line' like '*SystemRestore*' and 'Command Line' like '*disable*')
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Turning off services using sc exe
rules.description: This query checks for attempts to turn off at least 10 existing services using sc.exe.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ('Command Line' like '*sc*' and 'Command Line' like '*config*' and 'Command Line' like '*disabled*') | timestats span = 5minute distinctcount('Command Line') as ScDisableCount, unique('Command Line') as ScDisableList by Entity | where ScDisableCount > 10
references: https://github.com/Azure/Azure-Sentinel/blob/63ff8eedc58e7df0d22eba05ca73c92b59a66634/Hunting Queries/Microsoft 365 Defender/Ransomware/Turning off services using sc exe.yaml
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: umworkerprocess-unusual-subprocess-activity
rules.description:
This query was originally published in the threat analytics report, "Exchange Server zero-days exploited in the wild".
In early March 2021, Microsoft released patches for four different zero-day vulnerabilities affecting Microsoft Exchange Server. The vulnerabilities were being used in a coordinated attack. For more information on the vulnerabilities, visit the following links:
1. CVE-2021-26855
2. CVE-2021-26857
3. CVE-2021-26858
4. CVE-2021-27065
The following query surfaces when unusual subprocesses were launched by MWorkerProcess, the Exchange Unified Messaging service. This might indicate exploitation of CVE-2021-26857 to run arbitrary code.
More queries related to this threat can be found under the See also section of this page.
Reference - https://msrc-blog.microsoft.com/2021/03/02/multiple-security-updates-released-for-exchange-server/
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ('Parent Process Name' = 'UMWorkerProcess.exe') and ('Process Name' not in ('wermgr.exe', 'WerFault.exe'))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: UMWorkerProcess Creating Webshell
rules.description: This query detects unusual file content created by UMWorkerProcess, indicating exploitation of CVE-2021-26858 to generate a web shell. More related queries can be found on the Microsoft Security Response Center blog.
rules.oci_query: 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' and ('Parent Process Name' = 'UMWorkerProcess.exe') and ('Process Name' not in ('CacheCleanup.bin', 'cleanup.bin')) and (not ('Process Name' like '*.txt')) and (not ('Process Name' like '*.LOG')) and (not ('Process Name' like '*.cfg'))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: VMWare-LPE-2022-22960
rules.description:
The query checks process command being placed into the script; CVE-2022-22960 allows a user to write to it and be executed as root.
This vulnerability of VMware Workspace ONE Access, Identity Manager and vRealize Automation contain a privilege escalation vulnerability due to improper permissions in support scripts.
CVE: CVE-2022-22960.
Read more here:.
https://www.cisa.gov/uscert/ncas/alerts/aa22-138b
https://www.vmware.com/security/advisories/VMSA-2022-0011.html
Tags: #exploit #CVE-2022-22960
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Security Events') and (('Command Line' like '*/opt/vmware/certproxy/bing/certproxyService.sh*' or 'Command Line' like '*/horizon/scripts/exportCustomGroupUsers.sh*' or 'Command Line' like '*/horizon/scripts/extractUserIdFromDatabase.sh*') or ('Process Name' like '*certproxyService.sh*' or 'Process Name' like '*exportCustomGroupUsers.sh*' or 'Process Name' like '*extractUserIdFromDatabase.sh *')) | fields Time, 'Host Name (Server)', 'Process Name', 'Command Line', 'Command Line'

rules.name: Webserver Executing Suspicious Applications
rules.description:
This query looks for common webserver process names and identifies any processes launched using a scripting language (cmd, powershell, wscript, cscript), common initial profiling commands (net \ net1 \ whoami \ ping \ ipconfig),or admin commands (sc).  Note that seeing thisactivity doesn't immediately mean you have a breach, though you might consider  reviewing and honing the where clause to fit your specific web applications.
Those who don't mind false positives should consider also adding database process names to this list as well (i.e. sqlservr.exe) to identify potential abuse of xp_cmdshell.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Microsoft Defender Endpoint Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ('Parent Process Name' in ('w3wp.exe', 'httpd.exe')) and ('Process Name' in ('cmd.exe', 'powershell.exe', 'cscript.exe', 'wscript.exe', 'net.exe', 'net1.exe', 'ping.exe', 'whoami.exe')) | stats count as instances by 'Command Line', 'Target Filename', 'Host Name (Server)', Entity | sort instances
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Windows Anitivirus and EDR Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability
rules.description:
The query for malicious file creations via TOCTOU Vulnerability in Leading Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) and Antivirus (AV) Solutions.
- Microsoft Defender (CVE-2022-37971)
- Defender for Endpoint (CVE-2022-37971)
- SentinelOne EDR
- TrendMicro Apex One (CVE-2022-45797)
- Avast Antivirus (CVE-2022-4173)
- AVG Antivirus (CVE-2022-4173)
rules.oci_query: 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' and (Action = 'FileCreated') and ('Process Name' like '*ndis.sys') and ('Target Filename' like 'C:\\\\temp\\\\Windows\\\\System32\\\\drivers\\\\*')
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Windows Print Spooler Service Suspicious File Creation
rules.description: The query digs in Windows print spooler drivers folder for any file creations. This behavior is used from PoC Exploit of CVE-2021-34527, CVE-2021-1675 or CVE-2022-21999.
rules.oci_query: 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' and (Action = 'FileCreated') and ('Process Name' like '*.dll') and ('Target Filename' like 'C:\\\\WINDOWS\\\\SYSTEM32\\\\SPOOL\\\\drivers\\\\x64\\\\\\3\\\\*' or 'Target Filename' like 'C:\\\\WINDOWS\\\\SYSTEM32\\\\SPOOL\\\\drivers\\\\x64\\\\\\4\\\\*')

rules.name: winrar-cve-2018-20250-ace-files
rules.description:
This query was originally published in the threat analytics report, WinRAR CVE-2018-20250 exploit
WinRAR is a third-party file compressing application. Versions 5.61 and earlier contained a flaw that could be exploited by an attacker to read and write to an arbitrary path on the target's system. This could be used to run arbitrary code, overwrite system files, or access sensitive information. This vulnerability was designated CVE-2018-20250, and it is associated an outdated version of the legacy ACE compression library, 'unacev2.dll'.
The following query detects possible CVE-2020-20250 exploitation by looking for files with the .ace extension.
Reference - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-20250
rules.oci_query: 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' and ('Process Name' like '*.ace') and (not ('Target Filename' like '*\\Trend Micro*'))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: winrar-cve-2018-20250-file-creation
rules.description:
This query was originally published in the threat analytics report, WinRAR CVE-2018-20250 exploit
WinRAR is a third-party file compressing application. Versions 5.61 and earlier contained a flaw that could be exploited by an attacker to read and write to an arbitrary path on the target's system. This could be used to run arbitrary code, overwrite system files, or access sensitive information. This vulnerability was designated CVE-2018-20250, and it is associated an outdated version of the legacy ACE compression library, 'unacev2.dll'.
The following query detects possible CVE-2020-20250 exploitation by looking for files created in the Startup folder.
Reference - https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2018-20250
rules.oci_query: 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs' and (('Parent Process Name' = 'winrar.exe' or 'Command Line' like '*.rar*') and 'Target Filename' like '*Programs\\\\Startup*')
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Operational Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ((('Command Line' like '*accesschk*' or 'Command Line' like '*sc sdshow*' or 'Command Line' like '*Get-ServiceAcl*')))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Service Stop via Net Stop

rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Operational Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ((('Process Name' like '*\\net.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\net1.exe') and 'Command Line' like '*stop*') and (('Command Line' like '*vss*' or 'Command Line' like '*sql*' or 'Command Line' like '*exchange*' or 'Command Line' like '*backup*' or 'Command Line' like '*veeam*')))

rules.name: Shadow Credentials Attack via Whisker
rules.description: Detects Shadow Credentials attacks using Whisker or similar tools that modify msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Operational Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ((('Command Line' like '*Whisker*' or 'Command Line' like '*whisker*' or 'Command Line' like '*KeyCredential*' or 'Command Line' like '*shadowcred*')))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Shadow Credentials: msDS-KeyCredentialLink Modified (Event 5136)
rules.description: Detects shadow-credentials attacks at the directory layer: a write to the msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute (Event 5136, schemaIDGUID 5b47d60f-6090-40b2-9f37-2a4de88f3063) adds an attacker-controlled key pair so PKINIT can mint a TGT for the victim. Complements the existing Whisker process-creation rule with the authoritative DS-change event.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Security Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Event Security Logs') and (('Event ID' = '5136' and ('Properties' like '*5b47d60f-6090-40b2-9f37-2a4de88f3063*' or 'Properties' like '*msDS-KeyCredentialLink*')))
false_positives: Windows Hello for Business / passwordless key enrollment
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: SharpRDP Lateral Movement
rules.description: Detects indicators of SharpRDP or similar tools performing authenticated RDP lateral movement.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Operational Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ((('Command Line' like '*SharpRDP*' or 'Command Line' like '*xfreerdp*' or 'Command Line' like '*rdesktop*')))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Shortcut Modification for Persistence
rules.description: Detects creation of suspicious .lnk shortcut files using PowerShell COM objects.

rules.name: SID History Added or Failed (Events 4765/4766)
rules.description: Detects SID History modifications via Security events 4765 (SID History was added to an account) and 4766 (an attempt to add SID History failed). Injecting a privileged SID into sidHistory grants stealthy domain dominance.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Security Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Event Security Logs') and ((('Event ID' = '4765' or 'Event ID' = '4766')))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: SID History Injection via mimikatz
rules.description: Detects mimikatz commands that inject a privileged SID into the sidHistory attribute of a controlled account (sid::patch, sid::add, misc::addsid), granting domain-admin-equivalent access. GOAD shows golden tickets with SID history across forest trusts.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Operational Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ((('Command Line' like '*sid::patch*' or 'Command Line' like '*sid::add*' or 'Command Line' like '*misc::addsid*' or 'Command Line' like '*Add-ADGroupMember -SIDHistory*')))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Silver Ticket: Forged Kerberos Service Ticket
rules.description: Detects forging of a Kerberos service ticket (silver ticket) using a captured service-account or computer-account hash via mimikatz kerberos::golden with a /service: and /target:, or Rubeus 'silver'. Unlike a golden ticket, it forges access to a single service without contacting the DC.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Operational Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and (( (('Command Line' like '*kerberos::golden*' and 'Command Line' like '*/service:*')) and (('Command Line' like '*/target:*' or 'Command Line' like '*/rc4:*' or 'Command Line' like '*/aes256:*')) ) or (('Command Line' like '*rubeus silver*' or 'Command Line' like '*asktgs /service*')))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Skeleton Key Domain Backdoor via mimikatz
rules.description: Detects mimikatz misc::skeleton, which patches LSASS on a Domain Controller to install a master password ("skeleton key") that authenticates as any account while leaving existing passwords working.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Operational Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ((('Command Line' like '*misc::skeleton*' or 'Command Line' like '*skeleton key*')))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Software Discovery via WMIC
rules.description: Detects software enumeration using WMIC to identify installed applications.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Operational Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and (('Process Name' like '*\\wmic.exe' and ('Command Line' like '*product get*' or 'Command Line' like '*qfe list*')))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: SSRF to Cloud Instance Metadata Service (Linux)
rules.description:
Detects outbound HTTP requests to the cloud instance metadata endpoint
(169.254.169.254) from web application processes on Linux. This indicates
Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) exploitation targeting OCI/AWS/GCP/Azure
IMDS to extract instance credentials or configuration.
Covers MITRE ATT&CK T1552.005 (Cloud Instance Metadata API).
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'SOC Linux Syslog Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Linux Secure Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Linux Syslog Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Linux Audit Logs') and ((msg like '*169.254.169.254*') and ((msg like '*python*' or msg like '*python3*' or msg like '*node*' or msg like '*java*' or msg like '*ruby*' or msg like '*php*' or msg like '*httpd*' or msg like '*nginx*' or msg like '*uvicorn*' or msg like '*gunicorn*' or msg like '*curl*' or msg like '*wget*')))
false_positives: Cloud-init metadata access during instance bootstrapping
OCI SDK calls using instance principal authentication
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: SSRF to Cloud Metadata Endpoint (169.254.169.254)
rules.description:
Detects outbound network connections to the cloud instance metadata service
(169.254.169.254) from web application or scripting processes. This indicates
Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) where an attacker exploits a web app to
access the OCI/AWS/GCP/Azure IMDS endpoint and steal credentials, instance
identity tokens, or configuration data.
Covers MITRE ATT&CK T1552.005 (Cloud Instance Metadata API).
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Operational Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Sysmon Network Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and (('Destination IP' = '169.254.169.254' and Initiated = 'true') and (('Process Name' like '*\\python.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\pythonw.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\python3.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\node.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\java.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\javaw.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\php.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\ruby.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\dotnet.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\httpd.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\nginx.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\w3wp.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\curl.exe' or 'Process Name' like '*\\wget.exe')))
false_positives: Legitimate cloud SDK calls from web applications (rare — most use SDKs, not direct IMDS)
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Startup Folder Modification
rules.description: Detects commands copying or creating files in the Windows startup folder.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Operational Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and ((('Command Line' like '*\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup*' or 'Command Line' like '*\\Startup\\*')))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Suspicious HTTP Method Usage
rules.description: Detects use of unusual or dangerous HTTP methods (PUT, DELETE, TRACE, OPTIONS, PATCH) that may indicate API abuse or security misconfiguration. OWASP A05:2021 Security Misconfiguration.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'OCI Load Balancer Access Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Load Balancer Access Logs') and ((('HTTP Method' = 'PUT' or 'HTTP Method' = 'DELETE' or 'HTTP Method' = 'TRACE' or 'HTTP Method' = 'CONNECT' or 'HTTP Method' = 'PATCH')))
false_positives: RESTful APIs using PUT/DELETE/PATCH for CRUD operations
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Suspicious or Empty User Agent Detected
rules.description: Detects requests with empty, missing, or known-malicious user agents. Automated attack tools often use non-standard user agents or omit them entirely.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'OCI Load Balancer Access Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Load Balancer Access Logs') and (('User Agent' = '') or (('User Agent' like '*<?php*' or 'User Agent' like '*${jndi*' or 'User Agent' like '*<script*' or 'User Agent' like '*() { :;}*' or 'User Agent' like '*shellshock*' or 'User Agent' like '*masscan*' or 'User Agent' like '*zgrab*' or 'User Agent' like '*censys*' or 'User Agent' like '*shodan*' or 'User Agent' like '*internetmeasurement*')))
false_positives: Internal monitoring tools with custom user agents
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Suspicious Scheduled Task Creation
rules.description: Detects schtasks.exe creating tasks that execute scripts or binaries from user-writable paths.
rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Events' or 'Log Source' = 'Windows Sysmon Operational Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'SOC Windows Sysmon Logs') and (('Process Name' like '*\\schtasks.exe' and ('Command Line' like '*/create*' and 'Command Line' like '*/sc*')) and (('Command Line' like '*\\Temp\\*' or 'Command Line' like '*\\AppData\\*' or 'Command Line' like '*powershell*' or 'Command Line' like '*cmd.exe*')))
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Suspicious Usage of base64

rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'SOC Linux Syslog Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Linux Secure Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Linux Syslog Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Linux Audit Logs') and (('Process Name' = 'base64') and ((msg like '*-d *' or msg like '*--decode*' or msg like '*/etc/shadow*' or msg like '*/etc/passwd*')))
false_positives: Legitimate base64 usage by system administrators
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Suspicious Usage of chmod
rules.description: Detects execution of chmod with SUID/world-writable permission changes.

false_positives: Legitimate chmod usage by system administrators
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Suspicious Usage of chown

rules.name: Suspicious Usage of curl

false_positives: Legitimate curl usage by system administrators
rules.author: Upstream contributors

rules.name: Suspicious Usage of dd

rules.oci_query: ('Log Source' = 'SOC Linux Syslog Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Linux Secure Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Linux Syslog Logs' or 'Log Source' = 'Linux Audit Logs') and (('Process Name' = 'dd') and ((msg like '*if=/dev/sd*' or msg like '*if=/dev/mem*' or msg like '*of=/dev/sd*' or msg like '*if=/proc/*')))

rules.name: Suspicious Usage of gdb
